Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient shows a partial radiologic response after FOLFOX‑IRI with three lesions disappearing and the remaining lesions reduced by ~40 % and becoming hypo‑intense on MRI (LiverMetastasesUnderSystemicTreatment → Partial response). This suggests that down‑staging is occurring, but decisive anatomic information is lacking: the exact number, size, and segmental distribution of the residual lesions (NumberOfMetastases, Maximum/MinimumLesionDiameter, HepaticSegmentsInvolved), presence of vascular or biliary contact (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, PresenceOfBiliaryStructuresInvolved), and the future liver remnant ratio (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery) are all marked as Missing. Moreover, extra‑hepatic disease has not been ruled out (all Extrahepatic items are Missing) and the status of the rectal primary (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected?) is unknown. Because these missing data are essential to determine whether a curative liver‑first or simultaneous resection can be performed safely, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” – resection will be possible only after (a) completion of full staging (thoraco‑abdominal CT, detailed liver MRI with segmental mapping) and (b) confirmation that an adequate FLR can be preserved (or that portal vein embolization can be planned).  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Continue conversion systemic therapy (FOLFOX‑IRI or an alternative regimen) for at least 2–3 additional cycles while monitoring CEA trend and repeat liver MRI to document further tumor shrinkage.  
2. Obtain comprehensive staging:  
   • Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, or brain metastases (Extrahepatic items).  
   • High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and arterial phase imaging to define residual lesion size, segmental location, vascular/biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
3. Re‑assess resectability after imaging:  
   • If all residual lesions are confined to ≤4 liver segments with a projected FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected), plan curative liver resection.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) as appropriate.  
4. Address the rectal primary:  
   • If the primary tumor has not been resected, consider neoadjuvant long‑course chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) either before or after liver surgery, depending on timing and patient fitness.  
   • If the primary is already resected, ensure clear margins and assess need for adjuvant CRT based on pathology (grade, molecular phenotype).  
5. Surgical sequence (once resectability confirmed):  
   • Preferred approach is simultaneous resection of the rectal primary (if TME is indicated) and liver metastases when the liver surgery is limited (≤ 2‑3 segments) and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  
   • For extensive liver disease requiring major hepatectomy, perform a staged approach: first liver resection (or PVE → resection) followed by delayed TME after recovery.  
6. Post‑operative systemic therapy: resume or switch to an adjuvant regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for at least 6 months, guided by molecular profile (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF, MSI) once available.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation and molecular phenotype of the rectal tumor (GradeOfDifferentation, MolecularPhenotype).  
- Status of primary tumor resection (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected?).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
- Exact number, size, and hepatic segment distribution of residual lesions (Maximum/MinimumLesionDiameter, HepaticSegmentsInvolved).  
- Presence of vascular or biliary invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, PresenceOfBiliaryStructuresInvolved).  
- Future liver remnant ratio or volumetric data (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery).  
- Results of thoraco‑abdominal imaging to rule out extra‑hepatic disease (all Extrahepatic items).  
- Trend in CEA level during chemotherapy (CEALevelDecrease).  

These items are essential to confirm curative resectability, to plan the extent of liver resection, to decide on the need for portal vein embolization, and to determine the optimal sequencing of primary‑tumor and liver surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI.
B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
E. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor.
F. a chest CT scan
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation
I. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
J. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Recommendation 1 is significantly more comprehensive, covering resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy continuation, surgical sequencing (including simultaneous vs staged approach, PVE/ALPPS), management of the rectal primary (CRT/TME), and postoperative adjuvant therapy with molecular guidance. Recommendation 2 omits postoperative systemic therapy planning, neoadjuvant CRT for the rectal primary, and PVE/ALPPS considerations, while adding liquid biopsy elements not present in Recommendation 1. These differences represent significant gaps in clinical domain coverage. Step-by-step concordance: Both recommendations agree on the 'potentially resectable' classification (Step 1) and propose the same general management sequence: restaging with liver MRI and chest CT, FLR calculation, segmental mapping, and proceeding to surgery if complete clearance is feasible or continuing systemic therapy if not (Step 2). The core clinical reasoning steps are aligned. Case-tailoring concordance: Recommendation 1 explicitly addresses molecular profile implications (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF, MSI) for adjuvant therapy sequencing, lesion-specific surgical considerations (simultaneous vs staged resection based on hepatectomy extent), and patient fitness factors. Recommendation 2 mentions minimally invasive surgical approaches and liquid biopsies (ctDNA/CTCs) not present in Recommendation 1, while lacking detail on rectal primary management sequencing. These differences in case-specific clinical details indicate misalignment. Missing data concordance: Both recommendations identify the same core missing information: segmental distribution and precise localization of residual/disappeared lesions, FLR, vascular/biliary relationships, rectal primary status, chest CT, molecular profile/MSI, and CEA evolution. Recommendation 2 adds liquid biopsy (ctDNA/CTCs) as missing data, which is not mentioned in Recommendation 1, but the majority of essential missing data items overlap substantially, supporting overall concordance.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient now has three residual liver lesions each <2 cm after a major response to chemotherapy, which is compatible with a curative‑intent liver resection. However, decisive information required to confirm feasibility is missing: (a) whether the rectal primary has already been resected or requires neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, (b) precise hepatic segmental location of the residual lesions and any vascular or biliary involvement, (c) the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and (d) confirmation that there are no extra‑hepatic metastases on thoraco‑abdominal imaging. Because these specific prerequisites are absent, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Obtain complete staging: perform contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases that were not reported.  
• Clarify status of the rectal primary: if not yet resected, assess tumor stage (MRI pelvis) and decide on neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (long‑course RT ± capecitabine) followed by total mesorectal excision; if already resected, confirm R0 status.  
• Review liver MRI in detail (or obtain high‑resolution liver protocol CT) to map the three residual lesions to hepatic segments, evaluate proximity to major vessels or bile ducts, and calculate FLR volume.  
• If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic liver) and no major vascular/biliary invasion, proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmentectomy) aiming for negative margins (R0).  
• If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to augment FLR before definitive resection.  
• Schedule liver surgery either simultaneous with rectal resection (if both procedures are limited and patient fitness permits) or staged (rectal resection first, then liver resection after recovery), based on multidisciplinary consensus and patient comorbidities.  
• After surgical clearance, resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for a total of 6 months, considering addition of anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status, especially if postoperative CEA remains elevated.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Primary tumor resection status and need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.  
• Detailed hepatic segment involvement, vascular/biliary contact, and arterial anatomy.  
• Quantitative FLR ratio (volumetric assessment).  
• Results of thoraco‑abdominal imaging to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Grade of differentiation of the rectal carcinoma (affects prognosis and adjuvant decisions).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Both recommendations cover the same major clinical domains: resectability assessment, preoperative staging (imaging), surgical management (liver and rectal), systemic therapy (pre- and post-operative), and postoperative surveillance. Both address FLR calculation, rectal primary management, extrahepatic staging, and adjuvant therapy. Step concordance: The two recommendations diverge at Step 1 - Recommendation 1 classifies the case as 'potentially resectable' pending missing information, while Recommendation 2 classifies it as 'resectable' (pending volumetric reassessment). This is a meaningful difference in the resectability classification. Additionally, Recommendation 2 places specific emphasis on 'disappeared metastases' and their management (resecting/ablating all original metastatic sites), which is a distinct surgical philosophy not explicitly present in Recommendation 1. These differences in both resectability classification and surgical strategy result in a lack of step concordance. Case tailoring: Both recommendations address RAS/molecular profile implications (Rec 1 mentions anti-EGFR in RAS WT context; Rec 2 mentions MSS/MSI), lesion-specific surgical considerations (parenchymal-sparing, FLR, staged hepatectomy), rectal tumor specifics (TME, CRM, MRI pelvis), and patient-level factors (Rec 2 adds prehabilitation/ERAS; Rec 1 addresses patient fitness). Both are well-tailored to the case. Missing data concordance: Both identify the same essential missing information: segmental liver lesion mapping, vascular/biliary relationships, FLR estimation, extrahepatic staging (chest CT/PET), rectal primary status, and tumor differentiation/grade. Recommendation 2 additionally mentions disappeared metastases localization, MSI/MSS status, CRM status, anal verge distance, and liquid biopsy, but the core missing data elements are substantially concordant.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the single progressing hepatic lesion (segment VII, 5 cm) could be removed, but definitive surgical planning requires (a) completion of thoraco‑abdominal staging (thoracic CT to exclude pulmonary metastases and liver MRI to define vascular/biliary involvement and exact lesion count) and (b) assessment of future liver remnant adequacy (FLR ratio). Until these decisive pieces of information are obtained, upfront resection cannot be safely planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging: obtain thoracic CT, liver MRI with contrast, and calculate FLR ratio (volumetry).  
- Verify status of the primary colon tumor; if still in situ, schedule curative resection of the left‑sided primary (either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, depending on patient fitness and extent of liver work‑up).  
- Review systemic therapy: given heterogeneous response and KRAS mutation, continue or intensify current chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) while awaiting restaging; consider switching regimen if progression persists.  
- If imaging confirms that the segment VII lesion is resectable and FLR is adequate, plan hepatic resection (segmentectomy or extended right hepatectomy) targeting the progressing lesion and any residual stable lesions that are surgically accessible.  
- If FLR is insufficient, proceed with portal vein embolization of the right portal branches to induce hypertrophy, then re‑evaluate for resection.  
- If vascular contact or other anatomic constraints preclude safe resection, consider local ablative modalities (percutaneous microwave/RFA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy for the progressing lesion, followed by systemic therapy.  
- After successful liver (and primary) resection, resume adjuvant chemotherapy for at least 3–6 months, monitoring CEA and imaging for recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoracic CT results (rule‑out pulmonary metastases).  
- Liver MRI findings (precise lesion count, vascular/biliary involvement, arterial anatomy).  
- Future liver remnant volumetric assessment (FLR ratio).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or still present, symptomatology).  
- Presence of vascular contact or invasion by the segment VII lesion.  
- Baseline and post‑chemotherapy CEA levels.  
These items are essential to confirm resectability and to finalize the operative plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Both recommendations cover the same major clinical domains: resectability assessment, preoperative staging (liver MRI, FLR calculation, extrahepatic staging), systemic therapy adaptation, surgical/local management options, and post-treatment considerations. Step-by-step concordance: The two recommendations diverge on the key Step 1 assessment — Recommendation 1 classifies the patient as 'potentially resectable' pending further workup, while Recommendation 2 classifies the situation as 'unresectable at this stage' given the multifocal nature of disease and heterogeneous response. This is a fundamental disagreement in the resectability determination, which drives different management sequences. Although both then discuss restaging and possible local therapies, the underlying clinical framing and consequent decision logic differ significantly. Case-tailoring concordance: Both recommendations address case-specific elements such as the segment VII lesion characteristics, the KRAS mutation (Recommendation 1 explicitly mentions it; Recommendation 2 refers to molecular profile), heterogeneous chemotherapy response, FLR assessment, and the status of the primary tumor, reflecting good alignment on patient-level factors. Missing data concordance: Both recommendations identify similar essential missing information including detailed liver MRI/lesion mapping, FLR volumetry, primary tumor status, extrahepatic disease assessment, and vascular/biliary anatomy. Recommendation 2 adds performance status, MSI/MSS status, and liquid biopsy, but the core missing data items are substantially aligned.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The current imaging shows a radiologic complete response of the bilobar liver disease after conversion chemotherapy, but key information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing. Specifically, a dedicated liver MRI (preferably with hepatobiliary contrast) is needed to rule out residual occult lesions, to define vascular anatomy and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. In addition, it is unknown whether the rectal primary has already been resected or requires definitive surgery (e.g., total mesorectal excision). Until these data are obtained, definitive resection cannot be planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted and hepatobiliary sequences to (a) confirm the absence of residual hepatic disease, (b) delineate segmental involvement, vascular contact and FLR volume, and (c) guide intra‑operative ultrasound planning.  
• Clarify the status of the rectal primary: if not yet resected, stage the rectum (pelvic MRI) and, according to T/N stage, deliver appropriate neoadjuvant therapy (long‑course chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced disease or short‑course radiotherapy) followed by total mesorectal excision (TME).  
• After the primary tumor is addressed, reconvene the multidisciplinary team. If the liver MRI confirms no residual disease and the FLR is adequate, proceed to a liver‑directed operation (laparoscopic or open) with intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any microscopic lesions; perform parenchymal‑sparing resections if lesions are identified, or forego hepatic resection and adopt a watch‑and‑wait strategy with strict imaging surveillance if the liver is truly disease‑free.  
• Post‑operative management:  
   – If hepatic resection is performed, consider adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOXIRI or a fluoropyrimidine‑based regimen) based on pathological findings and molecular profile.  
   – If no hepatic resection is performed, continue systemic therapy according to standard protocols for metastatic rectal cancer (e.g., maintenance with fluoropyrimidine ± biologic agent) and schedule regular CT/MRI surveillance every 2–3 months.  
• Throughout, reassess molecular phenotype (RAS, BRAF, MSI) and tumor grade once the primary specimen is available, as these will influence adjuvant systemic choices and eligibility for targeted or immunotherapy.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Liver MRI results (lesion presence/absence, vascular involvement, FLR calculation).  
• Status of the rectal primary tumor (resected vs. pending resection, local stage, symptomatology).  
• Histopathologic grade and molecular phenotype of the primary (RAS/BRAF/MSI status).  
• Detailed hepatic lesion characteristics (number, size, proximity to major vessels) that are currently “Missing.”  
• Brain imaging (MRI) to definitively exclude cerebral metastasis, given the “Missing” entry.  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning: Completeness: Both recommendations cover the same major clinical domains: resectability assessment, preoperative staging (liver MRI, pelvic MRI), surgical management (parenchymal-sparing, intraoperative ultrasound), rectal primary management, and postoperative systemic therapy. No significant domain is missing in either. Step concordance: Both classify the case as 'potentially resectable' after radiological complete response to conversion chemotherapy, and both propose the same sequence: liver MRI restaging, rectal primary assessment with pelvic MRI, parenchymal-sparing hepatic surgery guided by intraoperative ultrasound, and postoperative systemic therapy. Case-tailoring concordance: Both address lesion-specific surgical considerations (parenchymal-sparing, intraoperative ultrasound to detect occult disease), molecular profile implications (RAS/BRAF/MSI), rectal tumor response assessment, and coordination of hepatic and pelvic surgery. Recommendation 2 additionally mentions prehabilitation/ERAS and minimally invasive rectal surgery, and details rectal tumor response categories (complete, near-complete, incomplete), but both are sufficiently tailored to the same case-specific elements. Missing data concordance: Both identify liver MRI results, FLR calculation, rectal primary status, and molecular profile as missing. However, Recommendation 2 uniquely identifies patient performance status, confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging, and liquid biopsy/ctDNA as critical missing information, while Recommendation 1 uniquely identifies brain imaging as missing. These differences represent non-trivial divergences in the missing data identified, warranting a score of 0.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, history of bisegmentectomy IV-V. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VII (3.9 cm). No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The liver lesion is solitary (1 lesion, 3.9 cm) in segment VII, isolated on thoraco‑abdominal CT and MRI, and the MDT notes it is “anatomically approachable.”  
- Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V has already removed a substantial portion of hepatic parenchyma; therefore the adequacy of the future liver remnant (FLR) after a second resection is a decisive factor. The structured analysis lists FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing, which prevents a definitive “Resectable upfront” classification.  
- Additional decisive missing items are the presence of vascular contact/invasion and detailed liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin). Because these key pieces of information are absent, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending their clarification.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain volumetric liver CT or MRI to calculate the FLR ratio after a planned segmentectomy of VII.  
   - Perform liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and an ICG clearance test to assess functional reserve.  
   - Review the hepatic arterial and portal venous anatomy with contrast‑enhanced imaging to rule out vascular invasion.  
   - Verify the status of the colorectal primary (has it been resected? if not, plan for primary tumor resection).  
   - Consider brain MRI if any neurologic symptoms are present, given the missing brain metastasis data.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if FLR is adequate or after portal vein embolisation)  
   - Because the tumor is KRAS‑mutated, initiate a standard oxaliplatin‑based regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months. This addresses potential micrometastatic disease and provides a window to assess tumor biology.  

3. Portal vein embolisation (PVE) if needed  
   - If volumetry shows an FLR < 30 % (normal liver) or < 40 % (post‑chemotherapy liver), perform right‑posterior PVE to hypertrophy the remnant before resection.  

4. Surgical resection  
   - Once an adequate FLR and clear vascular anatomy are confirmed, proceed with a formal segmentectomy of VII (or non‑anatomical wedge if margins allow) using intra‑operative ultrasound to ensure ≥1 cm oncologic margins.  
   - Preserve as much functional parenchyma as possible given the prior IV‑V resection.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy) as adjuvant treatment.  
   - Monitor CEA and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for recurrence.

Because these data are required to plan a safe, margin‑negative resection of both liver and lung disease, the lesions are considered potentially resectable pending completion of these assessments and neoadjuvant systemic therapy.

   • First, curative‑intent liver resection (major or minor depending on segmental distribution).

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma, four liver metastases (1.5-3.8 cm) and nodular peritoneal involvement at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal disease, not curable upfront, discussion of induction chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the presence of nodular peritoneal disease precludes an upfront curative liver‑only operation, but resectability cannot be excluded because critical information is missing. Specifically, the peritoneal cancer index (PCI), extent of hepatic segment involvement, vascular contact, future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected are all decisive for planning a combined liver‑plus‑peritoneal cytoreductive approach. Until these data are obtained, the case remains potentially resectable after appropriate down‑staging and further staging work‑up.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain the missing staging information:  
  • Perform a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define segmental distribution, vascular involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
  • Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy or dedicated CT‑based assessment to determine PCI, sites of peritoneal involvement (including hepatoduodenal and hilar ligaments), and to obtain peritoneal biopsies for histology.  
  • Complete molecular profiling of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) and record tumor grade.  
  • Verify whether the right‑colon primary has been resected; if not, schedule a right hemicolectomy (either before or after systemic therapy depending on symptomatology).  
- Initiate systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR agent based on RAS/BRAF status) for 2–3 months with the goal of downsizing liver lesions and peritoneal implants.  
- Re‑stage with repeat CT/MRI and, if indicated, repeat diagnostic laparoscopy after chemotherapy to reassess liver disease (number, size, vascular contact, FLR) and peritoneal disease (PCI).  
- Decision algorithm after restaging:  
  • If liver disease is limited to ≤5 lesions amenable to R0 resection, FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury suspected), and PCI ≤10–12 with no involvement of critical ligaments, proceed to combined curative surgery: right hemicolectomy (if not already done) + anatomical liver resection (or parenchymal‑sparing resections) + cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC.  
  • If disease remains extensive (high PCI, unresectable vascular involvement, insufficient FLR), continue systemic therapy and consider conversion strategies (e.g., portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy) or transition to best‑supportive care.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trend and assess for treatment‑related toxicity; adjust regimen accordingly.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Molecular phenotype (RAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Status of primary tumor resection (already resected or still in situ).  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and arterial anatomy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatible with safe resection.  
- Liver MRI findings (to complement CT).  
- Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) and specific sites of peritoneal involvement (including hilar/hepatoduodenal ligaments).  
- Timing of liver and peritoneal metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
- FDG‑PET scan results (to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease).  
These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Moreover, no systemic therapy has been administered to assess tumor biology and response. Because a specific prerequisite (completion of systemic chemotherapy ± radiotherapy and completion of definitive imaging) is required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, the case is “Potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT):  
   – Systemic chemotherapy appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type rectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody).  
   – Concurrent or sequential short‑course radiotherapy / long‑course chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary, based on tumor height and sphincter considerations.  
• Perform comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months of TNT:  
   – Liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define lesion size, segmental location, vascular involvement, and to calculate FLR.  
   – FDG‑PET/CT to confirm metabolic activity of the pulmonary nodule, exclude additional extra‑hepatic sites, and assess for occult bone or brain disease.  
   – High‑resolution chest CT to detail the pulmonary nodule’s relationship to bronchi and vessels.  
• If restaging shows favorable response and all lesions remain resectable:  
   – Plan a staged or simultaneous surgical approach, depending on patient fitness and operative risk.  
   – First, address the rectal primary (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) after completion of neoadjuvant radiotherapy.  
   – Second, perform parenchyma‑sparing liver resection of the two metastases, ensuring an FLR ≥20 % (≥30 % if steatosis/cirrhosis). If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization before liver surgery.  
   – Third, perform pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge resection or segmentectomy) of the left lung nodule, either in the same operative session (if technically feasible) or as a separate staged procedure.  
• Post‑operative management:  
   – Resume adjuvant systemic therapy to complete the planned total duration (typically 6 months total).  
   – Consider maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy given RAS‑wild‑type status, especially if residual disease is present.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance (CT/MRI every 3–6 months) for early detection of recurrence.

• Full characterization of the pulmonary nodule: size, exact lobar location, relationship to bronchi/vessels, and FDG‑PET uptake.  
• Results of FDG‑PET/CT for whole‑body staging (including brain).  
These missing items are essential to confirm resectability, plan the extent of hepatic and pulmonary surgery, and determine the need for pre‑operative portal vein embolization or additional systemic therapy.

Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- The liver MRI shows a segment VII metastasis with >1 cm IVC invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: True). Such major vascular involvement generally precludes immediate resection without further planning or down‑staging.  
- Critical information required to decide feasibility is missing: thoraco‑abdominal CT for extra‑hepatic disease (ThoracoCTScanPerformed: False), future liver remnant adequacy (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing), and the status of the primary colon lesion (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected?: Missing).  
- Because these missing data are decisive for operative planning (need to confirm no extra‑hepatic disease and sufficient FLR, and to decide on simultaneous vs staged colon resection), the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending those prerequisites.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases.  
2. Assess liver functional reserve: calculate FLR volume on CT volumetry; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % after chemotherapy), plan portal vein embolization or ALPPS to augment FLR.

Initiate systemic therapy: start a 2–3 month regimen of doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with a biologic agent appropriate for RAS‑wild type disease (e.g., anti‑EGFR such as cetuximab) to (a) treat occult extra‑hepatic disease, (b) assess tumor biology, and (c) attempt to downsize the IVC‑invading lesion.

Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
The case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” because several decisive elements are missing: the primary colon lesion has not been reported as resected, hepatic segment distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and future liver remnant (FLR) volumetry are absent. Moreover, the patient has synchronous liver disease (six lesions 2‑4 cm) that typically requires systemic down‑staging before a safe hepatic resection. Therefore resection is possible only after (a) confirmation that the primary tumor can be controlled (resection or effective palliation) and (b) acquisition of detailed liver imaging and volumetry to prove that an adequate FLR can be left. These prerequisites place the patient in the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy for synchronous metastatic disease. Given RAS‑wild‑type status, a regimen such as FOLFOXIRI + cetuximab (or FOLFOX + cetuximab) is appropriate to achieve maximal tumour shrinkage and address circulating tumor cells.  
- Perform a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (gadoxetate) to delineate the exact hepatic segments involved, assess vascular/biliary contact, and allow precise volumetric calculation of the FLR.  
- Re‑stage after 2–3 months of chemotherapy: repeat CT/MRI, measure CEA trend, and reassess CTC status. If the primary colon lesion is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or at high risk, schedule a colon resection first (either open or laparoscopic, with primary anastomosis if feasible).  
- If imaging shows that all liver lesions can be cleared with an adequate FLR (≥ 20‑30 % in a normal liver, ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), plan curative liver surgery. Options include:  
   • One‑stage major hepatectomy (e.g., right or extended right hepatectomy) if lesions are confined to one hemi‑liver and FLR is sufficient.  
   • Two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if lesions are bilobar and FLR is marginal.  
   • Parenchymal‑sparing resections (segmentectomy/partial hepatectomy) combined with intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 while preserving liver volume.  
- After liver resection, consider peri‑operative (post‑operative) chemotherapy to eradicate micrometastatic disease, guided by postoperative CEA and imaging.  
- Continue surveillance with periodic CEA, CT/MRI, and, if indicated, repeat CTC assessment.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Primary tumor status: whether the colon cancer has already been resected and any obstructive/bleeding/perforation symptoms (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization, PresenceOfSymptomsForObstruction/Perforation/Bleeding).  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: specific segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, arterial anatomy (HepaticSegmentsInvolved, PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, ArterialAnatomy).  
- Future liver remnant assessment (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery).  
- Confirmation of liver MRI having been performed (Has liver MRI been performed?).  
- Information on any prior systemic therapy (Has a systemic treatment already been performed?) and timing of metastases (synchronous vs metachronous).  
These items are essential to move from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
